\section{Results}

All results in this section are computed from a single parameter sweep of the
simulated market, run both without and with capture. In the baseline regime,
$N=1{,}000$ agents interact for $T=200$ periods with matching-function parameters
$\rho=0.5$ and $\delta=0.5$, turnover $\eta=0.02$, reservation threshold $f_r=0.6$,
and initial network degree $k_G=6$; the first 30 periods of each run are treated as
burn-in. Around this baseline, I vary one parameter at a time
($\rho\in\{0,0.3,0.5,0.7,1\}$, $\eta\in\{0.01,0.02,0.03\}$,
$N\in\{500,1000,1500\}$, $f_r\in\{0.4,0.6,0.9,1.2\}$, $\delta\in\{0,0.75\}$,
$k_G\in\{4,12\}$, and, under capture only, the broker's capture accuracy gate
$\kappa_{\max}\in\{0.4,0.5,0.65\}$) and I sweep seven two-parameter
grids: the six pairwise combinations of $\{\rho,\eta,N,f_r\}$ and the
$\rho\times\delta$ grid (on the grids, $\rho$ takes the three levels $\{0,0.5,1\}$
and $\delta$ the levels $\{0,0.5,0.75\}$; the remaining axes reuse their
one-at-a-time levels). The design comprises 91 regimes without capture and
94 with capture, each simulated under five independent seeds
(925 runs in total). Reported statistics are
ensemble means over seeds, summarized by time averages over fixed windows within a
run: late means over the final 20 periods ($t\in[181,200]$), used for all reported
levels unless noted otherwise, and early means over $t\in[50,70]$, to quantify
within-run drift. Full parameter values are given in Appendix~A~\S10, and every
statistic and figure as well as this results section containing them are
reproducible from the saved sweep.

\subsection{The broker primarily provides assessment, not access}

Across the simulations, the broker is the dominant channel in the market.
Principals route most demand to the broker rather than to self-search: the
outsourcing rate as a share of demand is
0.93 at the no-capture baseline (late mean, up from an early mean
of 0.81), and it stays high across no-capture regimes (late
means of 0.73 to 0.98). Principals prefer the broker because
its matches are better. The realized value of broker-channel matches exceeds that
of self-search matches in 90 of 91 no-capture regimes, with
an output gap (broker mean realized output minus self-search mean realized output)
averaging $+0.42$ across no-capture regimes (late means). This is the model's
rendering of why relational work gets outsourced: the broker constructs better
matches, on average, than clients do on their own. Table~\ref{tab:baseline-measures}
collects these measures, and the assessment measures discussed below, at the
no-capture baseline and across no-capture regimes.

The broker constructs these better matches by providing assessment,
not access. The access fraction (the share of brokered placements between two
principals with no pre-existing tie) is low, with a late mean of
0.16 across no-capture regimes (down from
0.22 early), and it declines over time in
all no-capture regimes. Most brokered matches connect
principals who already knew each other; the broker's contribution is to identify
which of them pair well, not to bridge gaps in the network.

Moreover, the broker's assessment advantage comes from ranking candidates better,
not from accurately predicting the output of potential matches. On a held-out
sample of random partners (Appendix~A~\S8), the broker
orders prospective pairings well (rank correlation of 0.89 with
the true ordering at the no-capture baseline, late mean, and
$0.85$ on average across no-capture regimes)
but predicts output levels poorly (holdout $R^2$ of 0.65
at baseline, $-1.48$ on average across no-capture regimes). Principals are
weak on both, with a holdout rank correlation of 0.51 and a
holdout $R^2$ of $-2.63$ (baseline, late means;
$0.51$ and $-2.73$ on average across no-capture regimes). To pick the
best matches, the broker's services rely on a good
ordering of candidate pairings, even without an accurate appraisal of their
absolute worth.

Within the model, the broker acts not as an appraiser of general quality
(cf.\ Li~1998), but as a
matchmaker who knows which parties suit each other. Its value comes from the
ranking of complementarities, and it holds even where clients can reach
counterparties directly.

\subsection{How the matching problem shapes the broker's advantage}
\label{sec:matching-shapes}

Different markets present brokers with matching problems of different kinds. In
this model, recall that $\rho$ sets the composition of the match output, from pure
general quality to pure complementarity, while $\delta$ controls the complexity of
the complementarity component.
Interestingly, across no-capture regimes, the broker's structural position tracks $\rho$
while its prediction edge tracks $\delta$, and the two need not move together.

The structural measures vary with the composition $\rho$ and are nearly flat in the
complexity $\delta$. Broker
betweenness centrality, the share of shortest paths between principals that run
through the broker, is higher where matching is more complementarity-driven
(0.82 at $\rho=0$ against 0.12 at $\rho=1$; late means along the
one-at-a-time sweep, $\delta=0.5$), while at fixed $\rho=0.5$ it moves little with
the complexity of the complementarity component (0.69, 0.73,
0.75 at
$\delta=0,0.5,0.75$). The access fraction moves the opposite way from the centrality
(0.12 at $\rho=0$ against 0.24 at $\rho=1$). Under pure
complementarity ($\rho=0$), the
broker is more central but, in practice, bridges less: a larger share of its
matches re-pair principals already tied to each other.

Meanwhile, the prediction measures vary with the complexity of the complementarity
component, $\delta$. Ordering is what the broker
needs, and its rank correlation with realized output stays high across no-capture regimes
(0.91 to 0.95 on the simplest problems,
0.89 at baseline, falling to 0.67 at
$\rho=0$, $\delta=0.75$; Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}), well above the principals'
throughout (0.51 at baseline, $0.51$ on average
across no-capture regimes). Performance at predicting the
output behaves differently from ordering: the broker's holdout $R^2$ under pure
complementarity ($\rho=0$) is
$+0.85$ when the output is simple but strongly negative when it is
complex ($-2.43$ at $\delta=0.5$ and $-3.89$ at
$\delta=0.75$, late means), worse than predicting
the average and, on the hardest complementarity problems, worse than the principals
(an $R^2$ gap of $-0.94$ at $\rho=0$, $\delta=0.75$), despite
the broker seeing both sides of every match and pooling across the market. Ranking
which match is better withstands difficulty far better than predicting exactly how
good it will be, and the broker's ordering edge, though it narrows on the hardest
complementarity problems, is what persists across different kinds of matching
problems.

In terms of realized match quality across different matching problems, the broker
produces better matches than self-search wherever matching is
complementarity-focused, most of all where
it is also complex (the output gap is $+0.73$ at $\rho=0$, $\delta=0.5$,
against $+0.12$ at $\rho=1$; late means; Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}),
consistent with the idea that the broker matters most where match value turns on
complementarity. This follows neither structural nor prediction measures cleanly.
The broker's realized output
advantage is largest exactly in regimes where its ranking advantage over principals
is smallest,
in the hard complementarity regimes: at $\rho=0$ the rank-correlation gap is
0.32 at $\delta=0$ and 0.11 at $\delta=0.75$ (grid,
late means). This is likely because in practice, picking the correct winner more
often is what really matters to realized outputs in this model, not the magnitude
of the performance gap.

\subsection{Opportunity, behavior, and the production of structural advantage}

In almost all regimes, the broker's structural position strengthens over time while
the agent network thins. At the no-capture baseline, mean agent degree falls
(27.1 to 23.1, early to late means) and the
broker's betweenness centrality rises (0.60 to
0.73), and this co-movement holds in 86 of 91
no-capture regimes (Fig.~\ref{fig:position}). Agent turnover removes ties about as
fast as they appear, and the network does not densify: agent degree falls over time
in 90 of 91 no-capture regimes. This raises a crucial question:
why is the structural advantage not self-liquidating, even at low turnover (at
$\eta=0.01$, betweenness centrality still rises from 0.45 to
0.62)?

The answer comes from the fact that structural position is endogenous, produced by
which agents form ties and which agents go to the broker. A brokered match adds a
new agent-to-agent tie, after which the broker no longer lies on the pair's
shortest path, only when the two were not already connected. Hence the broker's
work densifies the network only when it
provides access, not when it provides assessment, and across no-capture regimes access is
rare and falling over time (Fig.~\ref{fig:position}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/fig2_position_work.png}
\caption{\textbf{Broker centrality and access fraction.} Left: broker betweenness centrality and access fraction over time at the
no-capture baseline, as 5-observation rolling ensemble means over
seeds; betweenness is measured every 20 periods. Right: one dot
per one-at-a-time no-capture regime, each a late-window mean over that regime's
seeds. Time starts at $t=30$ (end of burn-in).}
\label{fig:position}
\end{figure}

The pure-quality regimes ($\rho=1$) come closest to escaping
this logic: principals there match well on
their own, outsourcing is somewhat lower (0.87 against
0.95 at $\rho=0$, late means), and brokered matches are twice as
often access (0.24 against 0.12). Yet, in these
regimes, the broker's position does not really self-liquidate, as it never
accumulates in the first place: broker centrality is far lower to begin with (a
late mean of
0.13 across $\rho=1$ regimes, against 0.73 at
baseline) and stalls rather than rises. The access share still declines within
runs, and the network still thins in 13 of 14 such
regimes (the five exceptions above to the co-movement between agent degree and
broker centrality are of this type). Only
in the pure-quality regime with the highest reservation threshold ($f_r=1.2$) does
mean agent degree rise over time. Identifying regimes in which brokered
access dominates and densification erodes the broker's position, if any, remains an
open question.

The broker's structural advantage across no-capture regimes, measured by
betweenness centrality, is negatively correlated with the access fraction
(Fig.~\ref{fig:advantage}): the broker is most central where it bridges
least. Bridging opportunity and bridging behavior thus move in opposite directions
across no-capture regimes, another counter-intuitive pattern in light of existing theory.
Clients value the broker's assessment services and outsource in large numbers, and
the broker's ties to its many clients are what make it central; its advantageous
position, however, does not correlate with making more access matches. Because
access is low throughout (a late mean of 0.16 across
no-capture regimes, declining within runs), the densifying effect of the broker's
work is weak and its
structural advantage persists. Where brokering is assessment rather than
access, self-liquidation of the structural advantage need not arise.

\centering

minus self-search) against broker betweenness centrality and access fraction; one

\label{fig:advantage}
\end{figure}

Across no-capture regimes (late means), the realized output gap is positively
correlated with broker betweenness centrality, but negatively with the
access fraction and the broker's holdout rank correlation
(Fig.~\ref{fig:advantage}). This is particularly true along the dimension of
changes in the matching problem. Complementarity-dominated regimes ($\rho=0$) are
sparse
and brokered-assessment-heavy: principals hold fewer ties, outsource more of their
demand, and the broker is at once most central and most valuable, while providing
the least access (Table~\ref{tab:rhogroups}). Quality-dominated regimes ($\rho=1$)
sit at the other end of each of these measures, with the baseline regime in
between. Structural opportunity thus accumulates exactly where the broker's
matches are worth the most.

\subsection{Conditions and consequences of capture}

In the capture variant, the broker may stop working on behalf of a client and
instead buy that client's demand and place it as a principal.
How much it does so varies with the features that shape its advantage, and with
the risk it must bear.

Capture by the broker is most extensive where matching is
complementarity-dominated: the captured share of outsourced demand (late means) is
0.97, 0.96, and 0.93 at $\rho=0$, $0.3$, and $0.5$, and
lower where quality dominates (0.77 and 0.76 at $\rho=0.7$ and
$1$) (Fig.~\ref{fig:capture}). Along $\rho$, however, multiple possible sources of
advantage co-vary: complementarity regimes where the broker captures most are also
those where it is most central and its matches most valuable, even though its
ranking edge over the principals is there at its smallest
(Sec.~\ref{sec:matching-shapes}), so the design does not separate which of them
leads to capture. Capture rates are
largely insensitive to problem difficulty (0.99 at $\delta=0$ against
0.96 at $\delta=0.75$) and to the pace of agent turnover (0.99,
0.93, 0.94 at $\eta=0.01$, $0.02$, $0.03$).

The sharpest control for capture rates is the reservation threshold $f_r$,
which sets the inventory risk the broker takes on: the
captured share is 1.00, 0.93, 0.78, and 0.20 at
$f_r=0.4$, $0.6$, $0.9$, and $1.2$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:capture}). As $f_r$ rises, the
captured share falls monotonically while the
broker's loss rate on captured positions mounts (0.06, 0.16,
0.35, 0.52 across the $f_r$ sweep, late means).

Capture is therefore most extensive where matching is complementarity-based and the
risk of acting as principal is smallest.

Capture reorganizes the market (Table~\ref{tab:baseline}; Fig.~\ref{fig:dynamics}).
Because a principal
placement connects the broker to each side but creates no tie between the two
clients, the agent network thins out: at the baseline pair, mean agent degree
under capture is about half its no-capture level, while matches per agent are
almost unchanged: what changes is who gets connected,
not how much matching occurs. The broker's own betweenness is slightly higher.
The access fraction reverses, high and rising within runs under capture
(from 0.60 early to 0.83 late at the capture
baseline, against 0.16 without capture; it rises over time
in 72 of 94 capture regimes). In a
thinned network, the broker is increasingly the only path between principals. Yet,
the access matches do not undermine the steady increase in broker centrality: with
a very high capture rate, the absolute number of access matches remains small.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/fig5_dynamics.png}
\caption{\textbf{Baseline dynamics with and without capture.} Lines are 5-observation rolling ensemble means over seeds at the
baseline regime pair. In each panel, pale gray reproduces the corresponding series of the other
row, so the two regimes can be compared directly. The capture row's last panel
adds the captured share of total demand (dashed). Axes start at $t=30$.}
\label{fig:dynamics}
\end{figure}

Outsourcing is also lower under capture (late means of 0.70
against 0.90 across regimes), because of the interaction between
the pricing and decision rules. A captured client is paid its own historical
average realized value: at the capture baseline (late means),
captured clients are paid about 1.29 per slot, while standard
brokered matches realize 1.46 and the positions the broker
keeps realize 1.69. Since standard brokered matches realize
above-average value, clients tend to be less satisfied with being bought out by
the broker than with concluding a brokered match. In the capture baseline, mean
satisfaction with the broker channel falls from the early to the late window,
returning some demand to self-search, while in the no-capture baseline it rises
(Table~\ref{tab:baseline}).

Captured transactions freeze the clients out of forming new ties, and this lock-in
produces the thinned network described above. By the same token, capture removes
learning opportunities: principal placements are recorded only in the broker's
history, so principals learn from fewer matches under capture than without it
(2,102 against 4,810 observations per period, late
means across the 91 paired regimes; 55\% of matches
under capture teach nothing to the principals).

Yet, on measures of holdout prediction performance, the principals
perform no worse than without capture. At the baseline pair, their ranking is
essentially unchanged and their level calibration is better
(Table~\ref{tab:baseline}); the pattern holds across the 91 paired
regimes (rank 0.54 against 0.51; $R^2$
of $-1.41$ against $-2.73$).
One reading, which is not tested here, is that without capture, when outsourcing
is high, the clients' out-of-sample weakness comes mainly from learning on a
selected sample, the broker's top-scored pairings. Capture reduces the outsourcing
rate and makes the sample clients observe less selected. A fuller account of client
learning, with and without capture, is
deferred to future work.
